doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Overdubbing versus recording live in the studio
summary: On recording technology, Conniff discusses leakage, overdubbing and why he prefers all players live together.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah, talking about the process of recording music, I mean you’ve seen from your days with Bunny Berigan up until your most recent one hundredth album, which I wanted to mention, you’ve seen a great deal of change in the actual technology of recording. Do you think it’s affected the music in the way it’s written, the way that technology has changed the recording of it?

It has in this way, that well let’s see, it’s hard to answer that. You know I think overdubbing has changed things a little bit. Because I remember as long as I’ve been in this business you’re always learning new things. The very last album I did was this one here called “I Love Movies” which is a very new album. It just reached the market, and it’s movie themes, stuff like “Star Wars,” John Williams — I have two John Williams in, he’s great, I love John Williams, “Star Wars” and “Can You Read My Mind,” — talk about, you know, melody and bass line, now you’re talking about a musician you know. And all of kind of today’s movie themes. I was recording and I was going to overdub the singers on “Can You Read My Mind,” which had lyrics. Usually if I have lyrics — by the way, I do everything simultaneously. I’m going back, I went through — in the beginning I recorded everything simultaneously in the studio, and then I tried a period of time where I went to the overdubbing technique by going in, record the rhythm section you know, and then I’d bring the brass and then saxes or the brass in and record to the rhythm, or bring the saxes in and record to the brass and the rhythm, and then bring the singers in and add them on top of everything. And this — we’re going to get into a technical thing now, but we’re getting into something that really improves the quality of each section in that you don’t have the sound of the drums, like in the first recordings we did, I’m going back now into ‘56, the one you first heard. You don’t have the drums. When the drum catches a punctuation by the brass, he leaks into some of the other mics, which changes the drum sound, which changes things around. But leakage is not that bad. But when you do the rhythm tracks alone and you put the drummer in a booth by himself, all you hear on the drum tracks is the drum, no leakage. So in other words, you don’t get drums leaking into singers, like we used to have on “S’ Wonderful,” “S’ Marvelous,” “S’ Awful © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

Nice.” You don’t get brass leaking into singers, like we have on “S’ Wonderful.” You don’t get brass leaking into piano, and drums leaking into piano. And you get clean tracks on everybody. But you do lose something I think. You lose the idea of 28 people in the studio at the same time recording a piece of music and hearing what everybody else is doing, and how the finished product is sounding. With the brass overdubbing technique, you do your rhythm tracks and the drummers are hearing the guitars on earphones. The guitars aren’t next to him. He’s not feeling them the same. And when the brass come in to overdub to the rhythm, they’re wearing earphones. He’s not really hearing the trumpets next to him as much as he did — well he has one ear and he does hear out of here, he hears the other trumpet, but it’s a whole different ball game. And one has advantages and disadvantages, and the other has advantages and disadvantages. I prefer everybody live in the studio at the same time. If you need a little more singers on something that had words, overdub them. And you have a feeling of excitement and fun that is on the record that doesn’t get there by the overdubbing technique. Now let’s see, what got us into this — you asked about changes—

Well that’s why I thought we should mention overdubbing, because I think that changes it a bit. It changes the writing a bit when you think you’re writing for overdubbing and not for something else, you know not for live. I think basically the answer would be no, wouldn’t it? That you wouldn’t change a lot because of the techniques.
